sentences.text: This complaint is filed under Sec. 200 of Cr. P. C. for the offence punishable under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act.

2. It is the case of the complainant that: The accused and her family members being well known to the complainant, had borrowed hand loan of Rs.1,50,000/- from the complainant on 12.04.2021 for her domestic purpose, agreeing to repay the same within six months with interest at the rate of 2%
p.m.

Towards repayment of the said hand loan, the accused had issued the post dated cheque bearing No.330158 dated 12.10.2021 drawn on Corporation Bank, Race Course Road Branch,
Bangalore in favour of the complainant.

As per instructions, when the complainant presented the cheque through her banker i.e., State Bank of India, Rajajinagar 2nd Block Branch, Bangalore, same was returned dishonor with memo "Funds Insufficient" on 27-10-2021.
Thereafter, the complainant got issued legal notice to the accused on 17.11.2021 through RPAD.
The said notice was returned on 20.11.2021 with postal shara "Unclaimed returned to sender".

Accordingly, the accused has committed an offence punishable under Sec.138 of N.I Act.
3.

After recording the sworn statement of the complainant and also verifying the documents,
cognizance was taken against the accused for the offence punishable under Sec. 138 of N.I. Act.
The accused on receiving the summons has appeared before this Court through her counsel and she was enlarged on bail and her plea was recorded.
The accused pleaded not guilty and claimed to be tried.
Hence, the case was posted for evidence of the complainant.
4. The GPA holder of complainant got examined herself as PW.2 and got marked documents as Ex.P1 to 7.
Then, the case was posted for recording the statement of accused under Sec.313 Cr.P.C.
In the statement U/s 313 Cr.P.C.the accused has denied all the incriminating evidence appearing against her and claimed to be tried.
The accused has not adduced any evidence on her be- half.

During the cross examination of PW-1, the learned counsel has confronted documents and got marked as Ex.D1 to Ex.D5.
5.
Heard arguments of both sides and perused the records.

6. The following points arise for my consideration:
1. Whether the complainant proves that accused has committed an offence punishable under Sec.138 of N.I. Act?
2. What order?
7. My findings on the above points are as under:

sentences.text: It is the definite case of the complainant that, towards the discharge of the hand loan of Rs.1,50,000/- availed by the accused, she has issued disputed cheque and when the cheque was presented, same was dishonoued for the reason "Funds Insufficient".
Though the said fact was brought to the notice of the accused by issuing legal notice but accused has failed to repay the cheque amount.
9. To substantiate the contention, the complainant got examined her GPA holder as PW2 and PW.2 in her examination in chief has reiterated the averments made in the complaint.
ExP1 is the cheque which bears the signature of the accused.
It is deposed by Pw2 that cheque in question was issued by the accused towards discharge of liability.
The cheque in question was presented by the complainant through her banker which was returned with memo as per ExP.2 stating 'Insufficient Funds'.

Hence,
she got issued legal notice to the accused through RPAD, which is produced at Ex.P.3.
Postal receipt at Ex.P4, Postal cover at Ex.P5.

GPA deed at Ex.P6 and Ex.P7 is the bank statement of Ashwathanarayana in SBI for the period 01-01-2021 to 31-12-2021.
10.

In view of the principles enunciated in the catena of decisions of Hon'ble High Court and Hon'ble Supreme Court, it is evident that when once issuance of cheque with signature of accused on the account maintained by him/her is admitted or proved then statutory presumption in terms of Sections 118 and 139 of N.I Act shall have to be drawn.
Now, it is up to the accused to place rebuttal evidence to displace the statutory presumption available in favour of the complainant in terms of Sections 118 and 139 of N.I. Act.
The burden of placing rebuttal evidence to displace the statutory presumption is on the accused.
11. The accused has not adduced any defence evidence but by cross examining the PW.2 has seriously disputed the financial status of the complainant to lend sum of Rs.1,50,000/- to the accused.
She has disputed the service of legal notice to her.

While disputing the alleged money transaction held between her and the complainant and disputing the issuance of cheques for discharge of legally enforceable debt, the accused has taken the defence that she and her family members had chit transaction with one Lakshman who is the close associate of the complainant and at the time of chit transaction said Lakshman had collected blank signed cheque of the mother in law of the accused and her family members i.e, the blank signed cheque of the accused and her husband namely Manjunath.
Though the chit amount was paid to Lakshman but said Lakshman insisted the mother-in-law of the accused to pay higher interest.

When the accused and her family members refused to give higher interest, Lakshman has misused the said cheque through the complainant and filed false complaint against the accused so also against the mother-in- law and husband of the accused.

12. The learned counsel for accused while addressing argument on the question of financial stability of the complainant to lend Rs.1,50,000/-, has vehemently submitted that the complainant is house wife, she has no source of income, she has not produced her bank statement so also the bank Soraj vs Ramya on 3 January, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/150459425/
3 statement and IT Returns of her husband and daughter so as to say that her husband and daughter are financially assisting her.

The learned counsel further has submitted that the complainant has not produced any document to prove that she has house property and that out of the said property she is fetching rental income and she has not produced document to prove that the said property was sold out and the consideration amount of the said property was with her so as to lend money to the accused.
It is further submitted by referring Ex.D4 that the complainant herself is indebted to several other persons.

13. While disputing the hand writings in the Ex.P1 and comparing the hand writings in the Ex.P1 with the hand writings in the Ex.D1 to D3, it was argued by the learned counsel for accused that except the signature, rest of the writings in the Ex.P1 and Ex.D1 to D3 are in the hand writings of the complainant as hand writings in the Ex.P1 and Ex.D1 to D3 are similar and is of the same person i.e.,
of the complainant.

14. Coming to the first and foremost defence taken by the accused as to the financial capability of the complainant is concerned, it is relevant to refer here that the learned counsel for accused has produced entire document pertaining to CC No. 2710/2022 marked as Ex.D1 which includes the deposition of the PW.2 herein given on behalf of the complainant in the said case.
Hence, the court can very well rely upon the documents marked as Ex.D1.

If the evidence given by the PW.2 in CC No.
2710/2022 is read co-joint with the evidence of PW.2 in the present case, the PW.2 has deposed that her mother is an un-educated lady and she is house wife.
One of the daughter of the complainant is engineer by profession and the husband of the complainant is an employee.
The PW.2 who is the daughter of complainant is graduate.

It is deposed by PW.2 that the case filed by her mother was decreed in her favour and in the month of November -2019 the complainant had received sum of Rs.25,00,000/- from out of the said case and the complainant had withdrawn some amount from the bank and kept it in her house for the sake of meeting the medical expenses.
15. It is deposed by PW.2 that accused was introduced by the mother in law of the accused and accused was working in KSRTC Department.

As per the evidence of PW.2 at the time of lending Rs.1,50,000/-, herself, her mother and their driver were present and that complainant had savings amount with her and from out of the said amount she had given sum of Rs.1,50,000/- to the accused.
It is the suggestion posed to the PW.2 that her sister Chandrakala is married.
The PW.2 deposed that her sister Chandrakala is unmarried and she is Software Engineer by Profession.
It is deposed by PW.2 that since meager amount of Rs.1,50,000/- was given to the accused, her mother did not insist to execute DP note and loan agreement.
16. During the cross examination of Pw2 question was posed whether the complainant had received license to receive interest amount on the hand loan.
The PW.2 deposed that her mother has not obtained any license to that effect.
If the entire cross examination of PW.2 is perused, nowhere the accused has posed suggestion that the complainant is running money lending business so as to get license from the concerned department.
It is at the mutual understanding the accused had agreed to give interest at the rate of 2%.

If the complainant had deposited Rs.1,50,000/- in the bank she would have get reasonable interest, likewise the complainant had given hand loan of Rs 1,50,000/-
by charging interest .

In order to meet the financial crisis accused demanded the complainant for Soraj vs Ramya on 3 January, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/150459425/
4 financial help and accordingly complainant lend hand loan of Rs.1,50,000/- by charging interest .

Unless and until it is proved that the complainant is running money lending business without having license, the mere fact that complainant had lend sum of Rs.1,50,000/- on interest the court cannot go against to the case of the complainant to arrive at the conclusion that complainant is running money lending business without license.
17.
The learned counsel for accused during the cross examination of PW.2 has confronted documents as per Ex.D1 to D4.

Ex.D1 is the document pertaining to the case registered by the complainant herein against Sudha who is the mother in law of the accused in CC No. 2710/2022 u/Sec. 138 of NI Act for the cheque amount of Rs.6,00,000/-.

Ex.D2 is the document pertaining to the case registered by the complainant herein against Manjunath who is the husband of the accused herein in CC No. 2709/2022 filed u/Sec. 138 of NI Act for the cheque amount of Rs.5,00,000/-.
Ex.D3 is the document pertaining to the case registered by the complainant herein against one Venkatesh in CC No. 10521/2022 u/Sec. 138 of NI Act for the cheque amount of Rs.2,00,000/-.
The said complaint was filed on 06-07- 2020 and the disputed loan amount in the case was stated to have been given on 05-01-2019.
Ex.D4 is the document pertaining to OS No. 5143/2018 on the file of Addl., City Civil Sessions Judge at Bangalore.

entities.text: Addl., City Civil Sessions Judge at Bangalore
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: The said suit was filed by one Sri Balamurali Krishna S against the complainant for recovery of money of Rs.9,50,000/-.

The judgment and decree dated 30-10-2023 passed in the said case discloses that the said suit was decreed and the complainant herein who was defendant in the said case was directed to pay sum of Rs.9, 50,000/-
with interest at 9% per annum.

18. The learned counsel for the accused by referring Ex.D4 has vehemently submitted that when complainant herself is indebted to others the question of her lending money either to the accused or accused in the cases registered under Ex.D1 to Ex.D3 does not arise.

19. In the light of the contention taken by the counsel for accused, if the Ex.D4 is read in whole it reveals that complainant who is the absolute owner of the schedule property in the said suit had agreed to sale the property in favour of Balamurali Krishna for a consideration of Rs.48,50,000/- by executing sale agreement and received advance amount of Rs.3,50,000/-.

But the complainant earlier to the sale agreement executed in favour of the plaintiff had executed deposit of title deeds over the schedule property in favour one Sri G Ramesh for an amount of Rs.11,00,000/-.

In order to clear the encumbrance of deposit of title deeds, the complainant again received sum of Rs.7,00,000/- from the plaintiff and cleared encumbrance by paying sum of Rs.11,00,000/- to Sri.G.Ramesh.
Thus, the complainant had received in all Rs.9,50,000/- towards the sale agreement from the plaintiff.
But the complainant instead of executing sale deed in favour of the plaintiff had already sold the property in favour of one Jayamma for a valid consideration by executing registered sale deed.
Hence, the plaintiff filed suit for recovery of advance amount paid by him towards the sale agreement.
From the aforesaid document it can be gathered that the immovable property of the complainant was sold in favour Jayamma during the year 2014-15 for a consideration of Rs.35,00,000/-.
Hence, the said amount of Rs.35,00,000/- was with the complainant.

Further the liability to pay Rs.9,50,000/- as per Ex.D4 comes in to effect from 30-10-2023 i.e., from the date of judgment and decree passed in OS No. 5143/2018 but not as on the date of lending disputed money to the accused.

Hence, it cannot be said that the complainant was indebted to others as on Soraj vs Ramya on 3 January, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/150459425/
5 12-04-2021 and that she had no financial capacity to lend sum of Rs.1,50,000/- to the accused as on 12-04-2021.

sentences.text: So far as the complaint filed by the complainant herein against the mother-in- law and the husband of the accused and one Venkatesh is concerned, it is the separate proceedings and in the said case the complainant has to prove independently her financial capacity to lend the amount mentioned therein and the legally enforceable debt.

20 . It is true that though the complainant has not produced her bank statement but the counsel for accused has produced Ex.D1, wherein the bank statement of the complainant was marked as Ex.P20 and Ex.P21 and the complainant has produced bank statement of her husband marked as Ex.P7.
Since the accused herself has produced Ex.D1 which contains the bank statement of the complainant, same can very well be relied upon even in the present case.

21. It is vehemently argued by the learned counsel for accused that when the amount allegedly given to the mother-in-law and husband of the accused herein was not repaid, the question of complainant giving hand loan to the accused during the year 2021 does not arise and that no man of ordinary prudence would venture to lend money to the rest of the family members, when the hand loan given to one of the member is not repaid.
The PW2 has deposed that the accused has given assurance that she will clear all the debts and by reposing confidence on the accused, hand loan of Rs.1,50,000/- was given to the accused.
22. Now at this juncture it would be relevant to refer here the document produced by the accused marked as Ex.D5.

Ex.D5 is the private complaint lodged by the complainant herein against the accused herein, her husband and mother-in-law alleging that the accused by borrowing sum of Rs.1,50,000/-, her husband by borrowing sum of Rs.5,00,000 and her mother-in-law by borrowing sum of Rs.6,00,000/- have failed to repay the amount with an intention to cheat the complainant and thereby committed offence punishable u/Sec. 420 of IPC.
The said compliant was filed in year 2021.
Admittedly, the private complaint was referred to jurisdictional PS for investigation.
After investigation B report was filed.
As per the evidence of PW.2 they have challenged the B report by filing protest petition and same is pending for consideration.

It goes to show that prior to the filing of the complaint u/Sec. 138 of NI Act, the complainant had presented private complaint against the accused herein and her family members alleging the hand loan received by them from the complainant and their failure to repay the said amount.

23. The learned counsel for the accused has submitted that the ink used for writing the contents of the disputed cheque and the ink used for writing the signatures in the disputed cheque are entirely different.

The learned counsel in further by referring the writings in the Ex.P1and cheques produced in Ex.D1 to Ex.D3 has vehemently submitted that the writings in the Ex.P1 and cheques in the Ex.D1 to D3 are similar and all the said cheques are written by one persons and they are in the hand writings of the complainant.
24. The learned counsel at this juncture has referred the judgment reported in ILR 2014 Kar 6572 between H Manjunath Vs. A M. Basavaraju.

sentences.text: In the said case, there was no statement in the complaint as to when the amount was actually given to the accused.
Except signature all other entries are in different ink and made at different time.

The complainant has merely mentioned the Soraj vs Ramya on 3 January, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/150459425/
6 date of issuance of cheque without any material particulars of the transaction.
Under the given set of fact the Hon'ble High Court has acquitted the accused.
25. In 2011 (5) KCR 4223 between M B Rajasekar Vs. Savithramma.
the accused was acquitted on the ground that the contents of cheque were in different handwriting.
The signature of accused on cheque did not reveal that accused had filled it in her own hand.

26. The learned counsel for the accused during the course of trial had filed application u/Sec. 45 of Evidence Act to refer the Ex.P1 and Ex.D1 to D3 to the hand writing expert to ascertain that the author of the recitals in the Ex.P1 and Ex.D1 to D3 are one and the same and to ascertain the change of ink in the Ex.P1 and Ex.P1(a).
The said application was rejected vide Order dated 29-03-2025.

While rejecting the application reference was made of the judgment rendered by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in (2021) 5 SCC 283 wherein it was observed by the hon'ble Apex court that" even if blank signed cheque is given to the complainant yet the statutory presumption cannot be obliterated, because, legally, even a blank cheque leaf, voluntarily signed and handed over by the accused, which is towards some payment, would attract presumption under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, in the absence of any cogent evidence to show that the cheque was not issued in discharge of a debt.

27. Further in Crl.Appeal 200074/2016 between Smt.Vijayalaxmi Vs. Shanker Kodla it was observed that "Even a blank cheque leaf voluntarily signed by the accused would attract the presumption under Section 139 of N.I Act".

28. Though the learned counsel for accused has referred two judgments regarding the different ink used for writing the signature and contents but the judgment referred by the complainant is of the recent judgment rendered by the Hon'ble Supreme Court.
Hence, reliance has to be placed on the recent judgment rendered by the Hon'ble Supreme Court.
29. Admittedly the accused has not challenged order passed on application u/Sec. 45 of the Evidence Act.
30. In the present case, the accused has admitted her signature in the disputed cheque.

When accused has admitted her signature in the disputed cheque, even if the contents of the disputed cheque are in the hand writings of the complainant or any other person it would make no difference unless accused with cogent evidence proves that cheque was not issued in discharge of a debt.
Further there is no reason to believe that Ex.P1 is in the hand writing of the complainant because complainant is an uneducated lady and accused has not denied the said fact.
Even otherwise, from the mode of signature put by the complainant in the complaint and deposition etc., it can be made out that complainant is an uneducated lady.
The body of the Ex.P1 are in English language and the complainant has put her signature in all the documents in Kannada.
Hence, there is no reason to believe that Ex.P1 is in the hand writings of the complainant.

31. So far as the explanation given by the accused as to how the cheque in question has reached the hands of the complainant is concerned, it is the suggestion posed to the PW.2 by the learned defence Soraj vs Ramya on 3 January, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/150459425/
7 counsel that the mother- in-law of the accused had chit business with one Lakshman in the year 2020-2021 who is the close associate of the complainant and that at the time of chit business said Lakshman had taken the blank cheques from the accused, her mother-in-law and her husband and even though chit transaction was completed but Lakshman did not return the cheque and under the guise that the said cheque was lost, he postponed the matter and later he insisted the mother in law of the accused to give interest at higher rate ( 
  
  
) and when the mother-in-law of the accused and her family members refused to give meter baddi, the said Lakshman in collusion with the complainant filed false complaint against the accused, her mother- in -law and husband.
32.

sentences.text: If the said defence of the accused is carefully analyzed, it is nowhere stated how much of the cheques the accused had given to Lakshman towards the alleged chit business which her mother-in-law had with Lakshman.

Further when the transaction between Lakshman and accused and her family members is alleged to be of chit business, the question of asking for meter baddi does not arise because as per the own defence of the accused the alleged transaction between the mother in law of the accused and Lakshman was chit transaction but not the loan transaction so as to demand for higher rate of interest.
In a chit business the question of demanding interest and giving interest does not arise.
It is true that complainant is in contact with Lakshman but the accused has failed to prove that they had chit transaction with Lakshman and she had given disputed cheque to Lakshman.

If really Lakshman had misused the cheque given as security towards chit business then nothing prevented the mother- in-law of the accused who is a Government Employee or to the accused or to the husband of the accused to take necessary legal action against Lakshman.
But till this date accused has not taken any legal action either against Lakshman or against the complainant.

Further, as per the case of the accused her mother-in-law had chit transaction of Rs.1,00,000/- with Lakshman and sum of Rs.12,000/- each for a period of 10 months was given to Lakshman towards chit transaction.

If that being the case, there was no necessity for issuing one cheque of the accused,
three cheques of her mother in law and three cheques of her husband and ATM Card of the mother in law of the accused as security for such a meager amount of Rs.1,00,000/-.
It is vehemently argued by the learned counsel for accused that the complainant has failed to examine Lakshman as witness.

But this Court is of the opinion that when accused has asserted that her mother in law had chit transaction with Lakshman and that Lakshman has misused the cheques given by her mother in law , herself and her husband as security, under such circumstances it is for the accused to prove the same by examining Lakshman as her witness.
As per Sec.101 of Evidence Act the person desiring a judgment based on facts must prove those facts.
It is submitted by the learned counsel for accused that when accused has made allegation against Lakshman, he cannot be summoned as witness.

It is true that even if Lakshman was summoned as witness by the accused he may not give favourable answer but the accused could have taken steps to summon Lakshman as witness and in the event if he had given evidence against the accused, the accused could have cross-examined Lakshman by treating him as hostile.
Hence, burden is not on the complainant to prove negative point.
When it is not at all the case of the complainant that she has misused the cheque allegedly given by accused to Lakshman, the question of complainant examining Lakshman as witness does not arise.

So far as the defence taken by the accused that Lakshman was running chit business and her mother in law was member of the chit business for Rs.1,00,000/- is concerned, at first the accused has failed to prove the said defence.
Further when the mother in law of the accused is a Govt. Employee, it is not permissible for a Govt. Employee to invest money in an unauthorized chit business.

33. The accused having admitted her signature in the disputed cheque failed to explain how the cheque in question has reached the hands of the complainant.
34. The learned counsel for the accused during the course of argument has referred judgment in Dattatraya Vs. Sharanappa in Crl., A.No. 3257/2024.

In the said case, since the complainant failed to prove the financial capacity and failed to state as to when the loan was advanced and failed to explain how a cheque issued by the accused allegedly in favour of third party has landed in the hands of the complainant and since the accused had inscribed his signature on the agreement drawn on a white paper and not on a stamp paper, the Hon'ble Supreme court has dismissed the complaint on the ground that accused has been able to cast a shadow of doubt on the case presented by the complainant.
35.
The learned counsel further has referred judgment in Crl.A.No.939/2010 between Yeshwanth Kumar Vs. Shanth Kumar N.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The said judgment is also in reference to not proving the financial capacity.

36. The learned counsel has referred judgment reported in AIR 2019 SC 1983 between Basalingappa Vs. Mudibasappa wherein complainant has not satisfactorily explained the contradiction in the complaint vis- a - vis his examination in chief and cross examination.
But in the present case, there is no contradictory evidence given by the complainant.

37. If the judgment relied by the learned counsel for accused reported in AIR 2010 SCC 1898 between Rangappa Vs. Mohan is read wherein it was observed inter alia that "the bare denial of the passing of the consideration apparently does not appear to be any defence.
Something which is probable has to be brought on record for getting the benefit of shifting the owners of proving to the plaintiff".

To prove the presumption, the defendant has to bring on record such facts and circumstances upon consideration of which the court may either believe that the consideration did not exists or its non existence was so probable that a prudent man would under the circumstances of the case act upon the plea that it did not exist.
38. In 2013 (1) DCR 326 between Nandi Agro Fertilizers Vs. D Sathish

entities.text: Nandi Agro Fertilizers Vs. D Sathish
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: it was observed that "though a notice has not been replied by the respondent, though it could be a circumstances in favour of the appellant, but at the same time despite this circumstances in favour of the appellant, the doubt which arise stands unexplained.

Furthermore the Apex Court has held that the respondent has to raise a probable defence and if there are circumstances to prove the probable defence that itself it sufficient to dismiss the complaint.

The scrutiny of the decisions and the principles laid down are not applicable to the facts of this case and the probable defence that has been put forth by the respondent creates serious doubt with regard to the genuineness of the appellant.

Soraj vs Ramya on 3 January, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/150459425/
9 39.

So far as the defence taken by the accused that the disputed cheque was given by her as security for the chit transaction of her mother-in-law with Lakshman is concerned, if really the mother in law of the accused, husband of the accused and accused had given their cheques as security then Lakshman himself would have presented the said cheques before the bank and there was no necessity for the complainant to present the cheques on behalf of Lakshman.

40. Keeping the observation made in the aforesaid ruling coupled with the discussion made herein above it can be said that the accused has failed to made out probable defence so as to rebut the presumption raised in favour of the complainant.

41. So far as, service of notice is concerned, though the accused has stated that notice is not served to her but no where the accused has disputed the correctness of the address mentioned in the legal notice but stated that at the time of issuance of notice they were not residing in the said address but were residing in the address stated in her cross examination.
The accused has not produced any evidence to prove that as on the date of issuance of notice they were residing in the address stated in her cross examination.
Further, if the bail bond executed by the accused is perused, wherein the accused has given her address which is the address mentioned in the legal notice.

When the legal notice is sent to the correct address of the accused through RPAD, presumption shall have to be drawn under section 27 of the General Clauses Act regarding due service of legal notice .
42. On appreciation of materials placed on record it can be said that accused has failed to prove the defence taken by her and thereby to rebut the presumptions raised u/Sec.118 and 139 of NI Act.
Hence, considering the facts and circumstances of the case it can be said that the complainant has proved the case beyond reasonable doubt.
Under such circumstances it can be said that accused has committed offence punishable under Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act.
Accordingly, I answer point No.1 in the affirmative.
43. POINT No.2 :- The Negotiable Instruments Act is a Special Enactment, and the provisions of the Act prevail over the general provisions contained in Code of Criminal Procedure.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
In view of the principles enunciated in the catena of decisions of Hon'ble High Court and Hon'ble Supreme Court, it is evident that when once issuance of cheque with signature of accused on the account maintained by him/her is admitted or proved then statutory presumption in terms of Sections 118 and 139 of N.I Act shall have to be drawn.
Now, it is up to the accused to place rebuttal evidence to displace the statutory presumption available in favour of the complainant in terms of Sections 118 and 139 of N.I. Act.
The burden of placing rebuttal evidence to displace the statutory presumption is on the accused.
Unless and until it is proved that the complainant is running money lending business without having license, the mere fact that complainant had lend sum of Rs.1,50,000/- on interest the court cannot go against to the case of the complainant to arrive at the conclusion that complainant is running money lending business without license.

It goes to show that prior to the filing of the complaint u/Sec. 138 of NI Act, the complainant had presented private complaint against the accused herein and her family members alleging the hand loan received by them from the complainant and their failure to repay the said amount.
Further when the transaction between Lakshman and accused and her family members is alleged to be of chit business, the question of asking for meter baddi does not arise because as per the own defence of the accused the alleged transaction between the mother in law of the accused and Lakshman was chit transaction but not the loan transaction so as to demand for higher rate of interest.
In a chit business the question of demanding interest and giving interest does not arise.
If that being the case, there was no necessity for issuing one cheque of the accused,
three cheques of her mother in law and three cheques of her husband and ATM Card of the mother in law of the accused as security for such a meager amount of Rs.1,00,000/-.
But this Court is of the opinion that when accused has asserted that her mother in law had chit transaction with Lakshman and that Lakshman has misused the cheques given by her mother in law , herself and her husband as security, under such circumstances it is for the accused to prove the same by examining Lakshman as her witness.
As per Sec.101 of Evidence Act the person desiring a judgment based on facts must prove those facts.
It is submitted by the learned counsel for accused that when accused has made allegation against Lakshman, he cannot be summoned as witness.
It is true that even if Lakshman was summoned as witness by the accused he may not give favourable answer but the accused could have taken steps to summon Lakshman as witness and in the event if he had given evidence against the accused, the accused could have cross-examined Lakshman by treating him as hostile.
Hence, burden is not on the complainant to prove negative point.
When it is not at all the case of the complainant that she has misused the cheque allegedly given by accused to Lakshman, the question of complainant examining Lakshman as witness does not arise.
So far as the defence taken by the accused that Lakshman was running chit business and her mother in law was member of the chit business for Rs.1,00,000/- is concerned, at first the accused has failed to prove the said defence.
Further when the mother in law of the accused is a Govt. Employee, it is not permissible for a Govt. Employee to invest money in an unauthorized chit business.
